blocks.text: Picture a spreadsheet of exam scores and someone asks you to pull out every score above 60. You would not scan the list one number at a time and manually copy out the ones that qualify. You would ask one single question, is this greater than 60, against every row at once, and keep only the rows where the answer was yes. That question and answer step, run against a whole array in one shot, is exactly what boolean masking is.

blocks.caption: This is the entire idea of boolean masking in one picture.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972721-869157839.png
1. Introduction

This lesson is about filtering NumPy arrays by condition instead of by position. You already know how to grab element three, or a slice from index one to four, or even skip axes with ellipsis. All of that is basic indexing, and it works off position, off where a value physically sits in the array. Boolean masking works differently. It works off a condition, off what a value actually is, and it hands back only the elements that pass.

Two lessons sit right next to this one, so it is worth being precise about what belongs where. Fancy indexing, covered in its own lesson, also skips plain positional indexing, but it works by handing NumPy a list of exact integer positions you already know you want, like index 0, 4, and 7. Boolean masking never asks you to know positions ahead of time. It asks for a condition, and NumPy works out which positions qualify for you.
2. Comparison Operators Produce a Boolean Array

Start with the piece that makes everything else in this lesson possible. Run a comparison operator, greater than, less than, equals, on a NumPy array, and you do not get back a single True or False. You get back a brand new array of the exact same shape, holding a True or False at every single position, one answer per element.

code.content:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([55, 82, 91, 40, 67])
result = scores > 60
print(result)          # [False  True  True False  True]
print(result.shape)     # (5,), same shape as scores

blocks.alt: Comparison Operators Produce a Boolean Array
blocks.caption: A comparison on an array never gives you one answer. It gives you one answer per element.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972722-676736884.png
2.1 Every Position Gets Checked Independently

Nothing about position two affects the answer at position zero. NumPy walks the array and checks each number against the threshold entirely on its own, the same way it handles addition or multiplication elementwise. The 60 on the right side of the comparison gets broadcast across every position, so every element gets compared against the same threshold, and the outcome for each one depends only on that single number.

code.content:
print(scores < 50)     # [ True False False  True False]
print(scores == 82)    # [False  True False False False]
print(scores != 82)    # [ True False  True  True  True]

blocks.text: 2.2 The Boolean Array Keeps the Original Shape

This holds no matter how many dimensions the original array has. Compare a 2D array against a threshold and you get back a 2D boolean array of the identical shape, with True or False sitting in the same grid position as the value it came from.

code.content:
grid = np.array([[3, 12, 7], [15, 2, 9]])
mask = grid > 8
print(mask)
# [[False  True False]
#  [ True False  True]]
print(mask.shape)   # (2, 3), same as grid

blocks.alt: The Boolean Array Keeps the Original Shape
blocks.caption: Shape is always preserved by a comparison, whether the array is 1D, 2D, or deeper.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972723-264776372.png
3. Using a Boolean Array as an Index

A boolean array on its own is useful for inspection, but its real power shows up the moment you drop it back inside the square brackets of the original array. Do that, and NumPy pulls out only the elements sitting at every True position, and drops everything sitting at a False position.

code.content:
scores = np.array([55, 82, 91, 40, 67])
mask = scores > 60
print(scores[mask])            # [82 91 67]
print(scores[scores > 60])      # [82 91 67], the same thing written inline

blocks.alt: Using a Boolean Array as an Index
blocks.caption: Drop the boolean array back into the brackets and only the True positions survive.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972724-365862691.png
3.1 The Result Is Always Flat

Here is the part that catches people off guard the first time they mask a multi dimensional array. It does not matter whether the original array is 2D, 3D, or has ten axes. The moment you index with a boolean mask, the result collapses into a single flat 1D array. Only the matching values survive, and they get lined up one after another in reading order, row by row.

code.content:
grid = np.array([[3, 12, 7], [15, 2, 9]])
print(grid[grid > 8])           # [12 15  9], flat, not 2D
print(grid[grid > 8].shape)      # (3,), one dimension no matter what

blocks.caption: A 2D array in, a flat 1D array out, every single time you mask with a boolean array.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972725-441599779.png
3.2 The Result Is Always a Copy, Never a View

The indexing and slicing lesson flagged this exact fact ahead of time in its comparison table, and here it is in full. A basic slice like arr[1:4] hands you a view that shares memory with the original array. A boolean mask never does that. arr[mask] always builds a brand new, independent array, copying the matching values out of the original into fresh memory.

code.content:
original = np.array([10, -5, 20, -8, 30])
positive_values = original[original > 0]
positive_values[0] = 999

print(positive_values)   # [999  20  30]
print(original)          # [10 -5 20 -8 30], completely untouched

blocks.alt: The Result Is Always a Copy, Never a View
blocks.caption: Same square brackets, two completely different outcomes underneath.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972725-754910222.png

blocks.title: Same brackets, different rules
blocks.content: It is genuinely surprising that arr[1:4] and arr[arr > 0] look almost identical to write, yet one shares memory with the original and the other never does. When you are chasing down a stray mutation, checking whether the indexing you used was basic or boolean is one of the first things worth ruling out.

blocks.text: 4. Combining Multiple Conditions

Real filtering rarely comes down to one single condition. You usually want elements that satisfy two or three conditions at once, like a score above 60 and below 90, or a customer who is a certain age and above a certain income. NumPy handles this with the bitwise operators, the ampersand for and, the pipe for or, applied directly between two boolean arrays.

code.content:
scores = np.array([55, 82, 91, 40, 67, 95])
mask = (scores > 60) & (scores < 90)
print(mask)             # [False  True False False  True False]
print(scores[mask])      # [82 67]

blocks.caption: The ampersand combines two masks position by position, keeping only where both were True.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972726-588355082.png
4.1 Parentheses Are Not Optional

Python evaluates the ampersand at a higher precedence than comparison operators like greater than and less than, which is the opposite of what your instinct expects. Skip the parentheses around each comparison and Python tries to apply the ampersand directly between 60 and scores before the greater than comparison even runs, which either throws a confusing error or silently computes something you never intended.

code.content:
# scores > 60 & scores < 90
# TypeError, the ampersand grabs 60 and scores first, breaking the comparison
mask = (scores > 60) & (scores < 90)   # correct, each comparison finishes before combining

blocks.title: Wrap every comparison in its own parentheses
blocks.content: Make this a reflex any time you combine conditions on arrays. Every comparison that feeds into an ampersand or a pipe needs its own set of parentheses, no exceptions, because operator precedence in Python will otherwise combine the wrong things first.

blocks.text: 4.2 Why Python's and / or Fail on Arrays

It is tempting to reach for Python's own and and or keywords instead of the ampersand and the pipe, especially since those keywords work everywhere else in Python. On arrays, both keywords fail, and understanding why makes the whole topic click. and and or are not operators tied to a method NumPy can override. They work by calling Python's built in bool function on the whole object to decide which branch to take. Calling bool on an array with more than one element is ambiguous. NumPy has no way to collapse many True and False values down into the single answer that and and or demand, so it raises an error instead of guessing.

code.content:
# mask = (scores > 60) and (scores < 90)
# ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous.
# Use a.any() or a.all()

blocks.alt: Why Python's and / or Fail on Arrays
blocks.caption: Python's and and or force a single True or False out of a whole array, and that is exactly what breaks.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972726-267957339.png

blocks.title: Why the ampersand and pipe do work
blocks.content: The ampersand and the pipe are genuine operators in Python, tied to methods NumPy overrides, so NumPy gets full control over what they do between two arrays. It defines them to run elementwise, comparing position by position and returning a full boolean array, exactly what and and or cannot do.

blocks.text: 4.3 Negating a Mask With the Tilde Operator

Flip every True to False and every False to True with the tilde operator. This is the boolean array equivalent of Python's not keyword, and it is handy whenever it is easier to describe what you want to exclude rather than what you want to keep.

code.content:
scores = np.array([55, 82, 91, 40, 67, 95])
mask = scores > 60
print(mask)              # [False  True  True False  True  True]
print(~mask)              # [ True False False  True False False]
print(scores[~mask])       # [55 40]

blocks.text: 5. Assigning Values Conditionally With a Mask

So far every mask has been used to read values out of an array. Masks are just as useful for writing values into an array, and this is one of the most common patterns for cleaning up data. Put a mask on the left side of an assignment, and NumPy sets every matching position to whatever value you assign, leaving every non matching position exactly as it was.

code.content:
readings = np.array([10, -3, 25, -8, 14, -1])
readings[readings < 0] = 0
print(readings)   # [10  0 25  0 14  0]

blocks.alt: Assigning Values Conditionally With a Mask
blocks.caption: A single line finds every negative value and zeroes it out, wherever it happens to sit.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972726-450489119.png
5.1 Mask Assignment Mutates the Original Array

This is worth calling out directly because it seems to contradict everything from section three. Reading with a mask, arr[mask], always hands you a brand new copy. Writing with a mask, arr[mask] = value, never makes a copy at all. It reaches directly into the original array's memory and overwrites the matching positions in place. The square brackets look the same, but reading through them and writing through them are two entirely different operations under the hood.

code.content:
original = np.array([5, -2, 8, -1, 3])
original[original < 0] = 0
print(original)   # [5 0 8 0 3], the original array itself changed, not a copy of it

blocks.title: No copy involved this time
blocks.content: Reassigning with a mask does not build an intermediate array anywhere. It is the exact same trick as arr[3] = 99 for a single position, just applied to every position the mask marks as True at once. If you wanted the original left untouched, you would need to call .copy() before assigning into it, the same rule that applies to any in place mutation in NumPy.

blocks.text: 6. np.where: A Vectorized Ternary

Sometimes mutating the original array is exactly wrong. You want a brand new array back and the original left alone. That is the job of np.where, which behaves like a vectorized version of the ternary expression you already know from plain Python, value if condition else other value, except it runs across an entire array in one shot instead of one value at a time.

code.content:
readings = np.array([10, -3, 25, -8, 14, -1])
cleaned = np.where(readings < 0, 0, readings)
print(cleaned)     # [10  0 25  0 14  0]
print(readings)     # [10 -3 25 -8 14 -1], completely unchanged

blocks.caption: np.where picks elementwise between two choices and always hands back a new array.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973282-921837313.png
6.1 Feeding np.where Two Full Arrays

The second and third arguments to np.where do not have to be plain scalars like 0. They can be entire arrays the same shape as the condition, and np.where will pick elementwise from one or the other depending on whether the condition was True or False at that position.

code.content:
plan_a = np.array([100, 250, 80, 400])
plan_b = np.array([120, 200, 90, 380])
cheapest = np.where(plan_a < plan_b, plan_a, plan_b)
print(cheapest)   # [100 200  80 380]

blocks.text: 6.2 Mask Assignment Versus np.where

Both tools solve overlapping problems, and picking between them comes down to one question: do you want to change the array you already have, or do you want a new array while leaving the original untouched.

blocks.caption: One question decides it: change what you have, or keep it and build something new.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973284-783174195.png
7. Worked Example: Cleaning a Small Sensor Dataset

Put everything from this lesson to work on a problem that shows up constantly in real data pipelines. Imagine a temperature sensor that logs a reading every hour. Whenever the sensor fails to get a reading, it logs a sentinel value of negative 999 instead of leaving a gap. Every so often an electrical glitch also produces a wild spike far outside anything physically possible for the room the sensor sits in.
7.1 Replacing Sentinel Values

The sentinel value negative 999 is not a real temperature. It is a signal meaning no reading at all, and it needs to disappear before any statistics get computed on this data, otherwise it would drag the average down dramatically. A boolean mask finds every sentinel position in one line, and mask assignment swaps them out for something sane, here the value np.nan, NumPy's built in stand in for missing data.

code.content:
temps[temps == -999] = np.nan
print(temps)
# [ 21.5  22.   nan  21.8 145.   20.9  nan  22.4  21.1 -60. ]

blocks.caption: One mask, one assignment, and every sentinel value is gone from the dataset.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973284-217908988.png
7.2 Clipping Outliers

Two values left in this data are still not believable readings for an indoor room, 145 degrees and negative 60 degrees. Rather than throwing those readings away entirely, a common cleanup step is clipping, pulling any value outside a reasonable range back to the nearest edge of that range instead of deleting it. A mask combined with the conditions from earlier finds exactly which values fall outside the bounds.

code.content:
lower, upper = 0.0, 40.0
temps[temps > upper] = upper
temps[temps < lower] = lower
print(temps)
# [ 21.5  22.   nan  21.8  40.   20.9  nan  22.4  21.1   0. ]

blocks.text: NumPy also ships a dedicated shortcut for exactly this pattern, np.clip, which handles both bounds in a single call instead of two separate mask assignments.

blocks.caption: Instead of deleting the outlier, the mask pulls it back to a believable edge value.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973285-969218377.png
7.3 Putting It All Together
Here is the full cleaning pipeline end to end, from raw sensor dump to something safe to average, in a handful of lines, every one of them a boolean mask doing exactly one job.

code.content:
import numpy as np

raw = np.array([21.5, 22.0, -999, 21.8, 145.0, 20.9, -999, 22.4, 21.1, -60.0])

cleaned = raw.copy()
cleaned[cleaned == -999] = np.nan
cleaned[cleaned > 40.0] = 40.0
cleaned[cleaned < 0.0] = 0.0

print(cleaned)
print(np.nanmean(cleaned))   # average ignoring the missing readings

blocks.text: 8. Recap

A comparison operator on an array never returns one answer. It returns a whole boolean array of the same shape, one True or False per position. Drop that boolean array back into the square brackets of the original array and NumPy pulls out only the matching elements, always as a flat 1D copy, never a view, no matter what shape the original array had.

Combine conditions with the ampersand and the pipe, never with Python's own and and or, since those keywords demand a single True or False and an array cannot give them one. Assigning through a mask, arr[mask] = value, mutates the original array directly, while np.where builds a brand new array and leaves the original alone. Both are core tools for cleaning real data, exactly as the sensor example showed.
